messages.body_plain:
On 7/3/2014 2:00 AM, Dario Strbenac wrote:
> I am writing a R markdown document and I can't suppress the message from
> stat_bin "stat_bin: binwidth defaulted to range/30. Use 'binwidth = x' to
> adjust this." How can I make my report neater ?

You can not suppress ggplot from emitting the message, but you can keep
it from appearing in the markdown document (I assume you are using
knitr). Add message=FALSE to the block options and the message will be
kept out of the markdown.

> Also, is there any convenience syntax to specify something like
> range/50. I've only seen examples were people give a constant number
> to binwidth. It would be desirable if there was some nice syntax.

You can specify the width of bins (with binwidth) or the specific breaks
(with breaks), but there is no syntax for specifying just the number of
breaks (in a manner analogous to the default). You would have to
pre-compute one of the other two values.

I can see this as a useful feature, though. It could be implemented as,
if the length of breaks is 1, then that is the number of breaks there
should be. I don't think that would break anything (since a single break
can't produce any bins anyway), but I'm also leery of that because some
functions that have similar behavior (like sample) can give headaches
when the behavior is triggered unintentionally. Alternatively, a
separate argument could be created (with defined precedence with regard
to binwidth and breaks).

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

aes call, but a reference to a column in a supplied data frame

ggplot(data=model12) +
   geom_point(size=2.5, aes(colour=factor(cluster)))

data in data.frame's. There are helper functions to get data in several
common format into a data.frame for use with ggplot (see the fortify
family of functions), but you need to know what each does to know what

I don't want to be more Catholic than the pope (if that's an international expression, and please I am not making any statement about this or any other religion), but:

the amount of discussion that goes into how to 'surpass' the warning is so much more than the energy needed to getting things done properly, avoiding the warning all together.

The degree of binning is crucial for how your distribution is being displayed: you're basically aggregating your data. If you get it wrong, you will misinterpret the shape of your distribution. Therefore: before you're going to plot your distribution, think about what's a reasonable degree of binning.

Below some code to illustrate what happens to the shape of the distribution if you change the binning. Note that these ought to be normally distributed data, and the distortion would be worse if you had skewed data.

set.seed(5)

df <- data.frame(x = rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 5, sd=1.5)) # create data

# create histograms with different bins: p1, p2, p3
# the second line in each plot adds title and fixes x-axis between plots
p1 <- ggplot(df, aes(x=x)) + geom_bar(stat = "bin", binwidth =  .1) +
  ggtitle("binwidth = .1") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,10))

p2 <- ggplot(df, aes(x=x)) + geom_bar(stat = "bin", binwidth = 2) +
  ggtitle("binwidth = 2") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,10))

p3 <- ggplot(df, aes(x=x)) + geom_bar(stat = "bin", binwidth = 3) +
  ggtitle("binwidth = 3") + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0,10))

library(gridExtra) # needed to combine the plots
grid.arrange(p1,p2,p3)

Best,

Richard

> I don't understand how to create and then plot with a simple function.
>
> In the static case, with fixed variables, the function is:
>
> dT <- -q * z * (1/kref - 1/k)
>
> I want to generate results for a range of k (0 to 5), and for a range of z
> (0 to 500), with fixed q (0.07) and fixed kref (2.5).
>
> I'm a bit thick at this though, and need some help.
>
> In long form I tried to do something like this:
>
> k <- c(0.1, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)  # can't have k=0
> k <- sort(rep(k, 6))

k = 0 produces a slope of -Inf. In ggplot2, you'd use geom_vline() or
geom_segment() to produce a vertical line.

>
> z <- c(0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500)
> z <- rep(z, 6)
>
> df <- data.frame(k=k, z=z)
> df$recip <- 1/kref - 1/df$k
> df$dT <- -q * df$z * df$recip
>
> Which doesn't quite get me where I want, as I want to plot "contours" of
> equal dT values.

Look at the first example here:
http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/stat_contour.html  It shows you that
geom_contour() or stat_contour() requires that the input data contain
(x, y) locations along with a height z.

So I thought I need a function for dT:
>
> dT <- function(k, z, kref=2.5, q=0.07){
>   dT <- -q * z * (1/kref - 1/k)
> }
>
> Except I don't know how to properly write it so that it's able to manage
> ranges of two variables.

AFAIK, stat_function() only works on functions of one variable,
similar to curve() in base R. You can get around this by generating
the function values in the data prior to invoking ggplot(). I did the
following for your data:

# Generates combinations of z and k values, returns a data frame
DF <- expand.grid(z = seq(0, 500, by = 100), k = seq(5))

# Defines the function value for each z-k combination
DF$dT <- with(DF, 0.07 * z * (1/2.5 - 1/k))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = z, y = k, z = dT)) +  stat_contour()

I don't know if this is anywhere near correct or not, but it's something...

Assuming this is at least approximately correct, if you want smoother
contours, increase the number of z and k values in the data frame
generation. If you want more or fewer contours, look at the bins or
binwidth arguments of stat_contour() or geom_contour().

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Wed, Jul 16, 2014 at 10:24 AM, Joel Schwartz <jo...@joelschwartz.com> wrote:
> I was trying to answer a question on Stack Overflow and came up with a
> ggplot behavior that I couldn't explain. I'm hoping someone here will have
> the answer.
>
> The questioner wanted to plot the following two data frames separately in a
> single plot using two calls to geom_bar:
>
> x <- data.frame(dat=rep(seq(1,4),3),let=rep("X"))
> y <- data.frame(dat=rep(seq(1,4),4),let=rep("y"))
>
> However, the code below results in the bars being plotted right on top of
> each other:
>
> ggplot(NULL,aes(dat)) +
>   geom_bar(data=y,fill="red",width=0.1,position = "dodge") +
>   geom_bar(data=x,fill="blue",width=0.1,position = "dodge")

In geom_bar(), position requires a mapped aesthetic to dodge, stack or
fill. You haven't supplied one. The 'solution' is to concatenate the
data frames, create a factor to distinguish them and proceed from
there.

This version dodges, but is ugly because dat is numeric, which
explains why you need to kludge the x-values:

x <- data.frame(dat=rep(seq(1,4),3), let=rep("x"))
y <- data.frame(dat=rep(seq(1,4),4), let=rep("y"))

DF <- rbind(x, y)
DF$let <- factor(DF$let)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = dat, fill = let)) +
   geom_bar(position = "dodge")

Another way is to pre-compute the frequency tables for each data set
and set dat to be a factor. This turns out to be more what ggplot()
expects.

x <- data.frame(dat = factor(seq(4)), freq =
tabulate(rep(seq(1,4),3)), let = "x")
y <- data.frame(dat = factor(seq(4)), freq =
tabulate(rep(seq(1,4),4)), let = "y")

DF <- rbind(x, y)
DF$let <- factor(DF$let)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = dat, y = freq, fill = let)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge")

Since data frames x and y have no way to 'communicate' with one
another, ggplot2's training process doesn't have sufficient
information to know that you want to dodge the two frequency tables.
You need a mapped aesthetic to dodge position, and in order to get
that, you have to combine the two data sets and make some preliminary
adjustments (e.g., redefining let as a factor with two levels) before
passing it to ggplot().

>
> I thought the following code would position the bars side-by-side on either
> side of each major tick mark. However, although the bars are separated, they
> are not symmetric about each major tick mark and the positioning of the bars
> is different at each tick mark:
>
> ggplot() +
>   geom_bar(data=y, aes(dat-0.05), fill="red", width=0.2) +
>   geom_bar(data=x, aes(dat+0.05), fill="blue", width=0.2)

This is necessary because (i) dat is numeric and (ii) you're plotting
the two data frames separately.

>
> But it turns out that adding + xlim(0,5) results in the symmetric bars I was
> expecting. On the other hand, a range of other xlim values result in some
> bars overlapping and some dodged. For example, xlim(-1,5) results in the
> first two pairs of bars overlapping and the other two dodged, but not
> symmetric about the tick mark. xlim(0.5,4.5) results in the first and third
> pairs of bars overlapping, while the second and fourth pairs are dodged
> symmetrically about the tick mark.
>
> Can anyone explain this behavior? Is there a way to reliably control the bar
> positions when plotting two separate data frames with separate calls to
> geom_bar?

If you have two data frames with the same variable names and the same
structure, it's easier to combine them as I showed above. If you
insist on combining separate data frames, you'll need to make manual
adjustments to make up for the lack of information ggplot2 requires to
do it programmatically.

Dennis

It turns out there is a way to control the bar placement. Brian Diggs posted this answer <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24769934/ggplot-bar-chart-with-two-dataframes#comment38468435_24769934> on Stack Overflow:

>   geom_bar(data=y, aes(x=dat-0.1), fill="red", binwidth=0.1)+
>   geom_bar(data=x, fill="blue", binwidth=0.1)
>
> The key here is that you are shifting the data by the same amount as one binwidth and that binwidth is less than the spacing between groups. The binning is done on the data after shifting, so that affects which bin the data appears in. Also, without setting the binwidth explicitly, how wide the bins are depend on the range of the plot (which is why it varies when xlim was varied and worked "nicely" for round values).

Dear all,

I'm plotting a map using ggplot2 and results are pretty neat, but there is one thing in the legend I need to change. Please take a look at this code, which is similar to the one I'm using except I have a actual map instead of a synthetic one:

library(raster)

       coord_equal()

messages.body_plain:
On 7/16/2014 8:58 AM, eipi10 wrote:
> I was trying to answer a ggplot question on Stack Overflow
> <http://stackoverflow.com/questions/24769934/ggplot-bar-chart-with-two-dataframes?noredirect=1>
> and came up with a result I couldn't explain. I'm hoping someone here will
> have the answer.

I've added an answer to the question there, but I wanted to give more of
a discussion of what is happening here.

> The questioner wanted to plot the following two data frames separately, but
> without having the bars overlap:

>
> x <- data.frame(dat=rep(seq(1,4),3),let=rep("X"))
> y <- data.frame(dat=rep(seq(1,4),4),let=rep("y"))

> He tried the following, but the bars are right on top of each other:

>
> ggplot(NULL,aes(dat))+
>    geom_bar(data=y,fill="red",width=0.1,position = "dodge")+
>    geom_bar(data=x,fill="blue",width=0.1,position = "dodge")
>

> I thought the following code would solve the problem:
>
> ggplot() +
>      geom_bar(data=y, aes(dat - 0.05), fill="red", width=0.2) +

>      geom_bar(data=x, aes(dat + 0.05), fill="blue", width=0.2)
>

> Although my code results in the bars being separated, they are not
> positioned symmetrically on either side of each major tick mark, but
> are shifted by different amounts at different tick marks. Can anyone
> explain what's going on and whether there is a way to control bar
> placement relative to each tick mark?

Realize what you are doing here is shifting the data *before* it is
binned. Now, this shift is enough to move it to the next bin over, but
you are not really putting two bins at the same value next to each
other; you are moving the data into different (adjacent) bins. The
visual effect is about the same, though.

What you are seeing with the shifting around the breaks is that the bins
are not what you think (I'm guessing you think they are 1, 2, 3, 4), but
rather 30 bins spread across the range of x values.

Consider your example

ggplot(NULL,aes(dat))+
   geom_bar(data=y, fill="red", position = "dodge") +
   geom_bar(data=x, fill="blue", position = "dodge")

The bins on this are

1   0.9  1.0
2   1.0  1.1
3   1.1  1.2
4   1.2  1.3
5   1.3  1.4
6   1.4  1.5
7   1.5  1.6

9   1.7  1.8
10  1.8  1.9
11  1.9  2.0
12  2.0  2.1
13  2.1  2.2
14  2.2  2.3
15  2.3  2.4
16  2.4  2.5
17  2.5  2.6
18  2.6  2.7
19  2.7  2.8
20  2.8  2.9
21  2.9  3.0
22  3.0  3.1
23  3.1  3.2
24  3.2  3.3
25  3.3  3.4
26  3.4  3.5
27  3.5  3.6
28  3.6  3.7
29  3.7  3.8
30  3.8  3.9
31  3.9  4.0
32  4.0  4.1

The data all fall in the 2nd, 12th, 22nd, and 32nd bins. And the bins
line up nicely on the round values. That is because the data is from 1
to 4, so the range is 3, divided into 30 bins give a binwidth of 0.1.
And if you put a bin boundary at 0 and then take the relevant ones (and
some padding), you get these breakpoints. But when you shift the data
before binning

ggplot() +
     geom_bar(data=y, aes(dat - 0.05), fill="red", width=0.2) +

     geom_bar(data=x, aes(dat + 0.05), fill="blue", width=0.2)

the bins are then

         xmin     xmax
1  0.8266667 0.930000
2  0.9300000 1.033333
3  1.0333333 1.136667
4  1.1366667 1.240000
5  1.2400000 1.343333
6  1.3433333 1.446667

14 2.1700000 2.273333
15 2.2733333 2.376667
16 2.3766667 2.480000

33 4.1333333 4.236667

This is consistent. The data go from 0.95 to 4.05, a range of 3.1.
Divide that into 30 bins for a binwidth of 0.1033333. All these
breakpoints are multiples of that binwidth. But that doesn't line them
nicely up on the integers.

Note that this also relies on the shift you are giving (0.05) is less
than the computed binwidth (0.103333) so that some data is shifted down
(no more than) one bin and the other data is not shifted out of its
original bin.

> I realize the "standard" ggplot solution would be to rbind the two
> data frames and use a fill aesthetic to get the two separate bars
> properly dodged (which is discussed in the SO question). However, if,
> for some reason, you want to maintain two separate data frames, is
> there some way to control bar placement when plotting the two data

> frames with separate calls to geom_bar?

The answer I gave at stackoverflow was

ggplot(mapping=aes(x=dat))+
   geom_bar(data=y, aes(x=dat-0.1), fill="red", binwidth=0.1)+
   geom_bar(data=x, fill="blue", binwidth=0.1)

This makes specific used of the shifting of data into different bins and
is explicit about the binwidth. One set of data is shifted one binwidth
(0.1), the bars are guaranteed to be separated. For this to work, the
binwidth must be smaller than the separation between unique values and
the values need to be multiples of the binwidth. If the data is not
quasi-discrete, this approach will not work, since there won't be empty
bins to shift the other data set(s) into. It will, however, generalize
to more than 2 sets (with the shifts being multiples of the binwidth),
so long as the product of the number of set and the binwidth is still
less than the separation between values.

> Thanks,
> Joel

--

> model for spatial data. I would like to visualize the mean and variance
> (error) of the data simultaneously. One method for doing this would be to
> use an HSL model for my scale_color_gradientn() where hue is mapped to the
> mean and either saturation or luminance is mapped to variance. Is it
> possible to map the aspects of a color to different variables in ggplot?
>
> For the sake of a minimal working example, I've borrowed from the
> documentation for scale_colour_gradientn().

> library(RColorBrewer)
> dsub <- subset(diamonds, x > 5 & x < 6 & y > 5 & y < 6)

You can change the color space within scale_color_gradientn() with the
space = argument, but you cannot map more than one variable to the
same aesthetic, which it appears you are trying to do. In other words,
you can't map color to diff for one purpose and then color to x for

messages.subject_clean: problem with coord_map() using large data
messages.body_plain:
coord_map splits each segment in small pieces and then projects them.
This makes it veeeryy slooow with geom_tile because it reprojects
every piece. It's not surprising that QGIS is much quicker.

You can try:
- coord_quickmap which only does an approximate scaling. Should be
enough for your region of interest
- geom_raster which creates a raster instead of vector tiles and is
faster (but writing this I realize that I am not sure it works with
something else than coord_cartesian).

JiHO

messages.subject: Re: Simultaneous visualization of mean and error in spatial data? (with example)
messages.subject_clean: Simultaneous visualization of mean and error in spatial data? (with example)
messages.body_plain:
It seems we use ggplot for similar purposes. I've been wanting to do
exactly what you want for a similar purpose (mapping model results).
There might even be a question about it in the archive of this mailing
list.

Unfortunately, there is a scale_fill_hue but not a
scale_fill_saturation. Writing it would make for a very nice addition
to ggplot but I could never figure out where to start. In addition,
ideally, the legend should be bidimensional, with hue on one axis and
saturation on the other. This is likely to be even harder.

The workarounds I explored were:
- mapping the result to color and the uncertainty to transparency
(alpha) making more uncertain regions more transparent, i.e. less
visible.
- creating a layer with colour mapped to the result and create another
layer with a solid grey fill but alpha mapped to confidence (1 -
uncertainty). The colour gradient should have the same saturation and
luminance, and vary in hue only (that's the case for the default hue
scale I think). The grey of the layer above should have the same
luminance as the colours (i.e. mimic the desaturation of one of the
colours). The transparency should be full for the points of high
confidence. Doing it this way, the uncertain regions are grey or
greyish and the well predicted regions should full colours.

Hope that helps.

JiHO

Here's one attempt. I changed Year to numeric because it makes no
sense to me to label every year over a 30 year span. Too much visual
clutter.

mydata<- data.frame(
  Year = 1980:2009,

  Type = factor(rep(c("stuff1", "stuff2", "stuff3"), each = 10*3)),

  Value = rnorm(90, mean = seq(90),

                sd = rep(c(6, 7, 3), each = 10)))

library(zoo)
library(plyr)

# rollmean() is a function from the zoo package that computes
# moving averages. The second argument indicates the number
# of values to average at a time.

f <- function(d)
{
   require(zoo)
   data.frame(Year = d$Year[5:length(d$Year)],
              mavg = rollmean(d$Value, 5))
}

# Apply the function to each group
madf <- ddply(mydata, "Type", f)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(mydata, aes(x=Year, y=Value)) +
  geom_point(mapping=aes(shape=Type), size=2) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_line(data = madf, mapping=aes(x = Year, y = mavg, linetype=Type,
                         color = Type), size = 1) +

  ylab(expression(paste("mean ",mu, "g",C~L^{-1}, day^{-1}))) +
  theme(legend.key = element_blank())

I’m new to R and struggle with the code of a multi-plot panel. I need to arrange 45 bar charts on one page with annotations at top, bottom and left hand side. I used ggplot2 to create the plots and grid to place the plots on the single page. I’m happy with the location of the plots and the annotations. I’m really unhappy with the margins between the plots. The margins between the plots are too big and the plots as such a far too small. I guess the source of the problem is in the grid.layout  function. Many thanks for your help!

Ulrika

messages.body_plain:
You haven't given us a reproducible example--e.g. a simple data set and code that runs it--which makes things harder. But:

-- You'd only get three geom_smooth lines if, in its (or the plot) aes() call, there was a 'linetype= P7APrior' or 'color= P7APrior' setting. Try adding this.

-- But...I don't understand why you're setting ymin and ymax in the aes() call, as geom_smooth() doesn't understand these aesthetics (see its help page).

-- What I suspect you want to do is ditch geom_smooth entirely, since you've already fit linear models in the code above, and use geom_line(aes(y= P7APrior)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lcl,ymax=ucl)). Or something like that.

Hopefully this makes sense and is useful. Again, for more specific help, please post a fully reproducible example.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Although I am not an expert in ggplot2, my first guess is that the difference is caused by not the order of stat and geom but the position = "identity". As the position is usually not an aesthetic variable, it does nothing inside of the aes() parentheses, and the default value of position is stacked, thus, during the call your position variable will be overwritten.

Compare

#1
p+geom_line(aes(y=..count.., ymax=..count.., group=cut, position="identity"),stat="bin")
#2
p+stat_bin(aes(y=..count.., ymax=..count.., group=cut, position="identity"),geom="line")

and #3
p+stat_bin(aes(y=..count.., ymax=..count.., group=cut), position="identity", geom="line")

By geom_line the default position is identity, this is why you cannot see the phenomenon there.

   geom_point() +

each other. You need the group aesthetic to produce lines across
factor levels, which works most easily when the factor is on the
x-axis. The coord_flip() call exchanges the x and y axes after the
points and lines are produced.

On Fri, Jul 25, 2014 at 5:41 AM, mrgreen88er <mrgre...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello ggplot2 mailing list,
>
> i want to plot data points with ggplot2 so that the data points which exist more than one time are shown in a different colour.
> For example: Data point occurs 2 times, plotted in red. 3 times plotted in blue and so on.

I'd suggest creating a data frame from a frequency table of the unique (x, y) pairs and pass that to ggplot(). Your table will need to be 2D. See either the table() function and as.data.frame(<mytable>) or the count() function from the plyr package; the latter returns a data frame by default. You may need to change the column names of the returned data frame depending on which function you used to generate it.

>
> This is my code:
>
>  ggplot(res, aes(res$freqStrategy, res$freqStrategyChanges))+

You don't need to reiterate the data frame; the following will do:

ggplot(res, aes(x = freqStrategy, y = freqStrategyChanges)

>  geom_point(alpha=0.5)
>

In the new call, you would use the frequency variable for color. If you leave it as numeric, the legend will use a colorbar guide. If you want the values discretized, you'll need to create a factor, possibly with cut(), that would represent the ranges of values associated with individual colors. This should also be done in the data frame prior to passing it to ggplot(). Something like

ggplot(DF, aes(x, y, color = Freq)) + geom_point()

Another option is to use geom_point(..., position = position_jitter()) to jitter the points if the repeats are rather sparse.

Dennis

messages.subject: How to determine the best dimensions for saving figure?
messages.subject_clean: How to determine the best dimensions for saving figure?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

In the last weeks I have been facing terrible problems when trying to save ggplot pictures. Specifically, it is hard to determine the resolution of the .png file when saving a grid with some ggplots. To me, It is usually a very tedious trial and error procedure, that most of times consume a much longer time than I would like (especially when writing chapters of a PhD dissertation).

To illustrate my problem, please take a moment to reproduce my code:

# load required packages
library(ggplot2)
library(raster)
library(gridExtra)

# Download data - ~1.5Mb
bra <- getData('GADM', country='BRA', level=1)
toc <- bra[bra$NAME_1=="Tocantins",] # subset Tocantins state from BRA map

# Extent rectangle for inset map
e <- extent(toc)
pol <- data.frame(xmin=e@xmin, xmax=e@xmax, ymin=e@ymin, ymax=e@ymax)

# Coordinates of micromet station
station <- data.frame(lat=-50.13, long=-9.816)

# Main map
m1 <- ggplot() +
      geom_polygon(data=bra, aes(long, lat, group=group), colour="grey10", fill="#cccccc") +
      coord_equal() +
      theme_bw(base_size = 22) + labs(x=NULL,y=NULL) +
      geom_rect(data = pol, aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                alpha=0, colour="red", size = 1, linetype=1) +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(-80,-30,5), labels=c(paste(seq(80,30,-5),"°W", sep=""))) +
      scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-40,10,5), labels=c(paste(seq(-40,10,5),"°S", sep="")))

# Inset Map
m2 <- ggplot() +
      geom_polygon(data=toc, aes(long, lat, group=group), fill="#9ecae1") +
      geom_polygon(data=toc, aes(long, lat, group=group), colour="grey10", fill="#999999") +
      annotate("text", x = -50.5, y = -11, label = "Araguaia River", angle=80, size=6) +
      annotate("text", x = -49.8, y = -11, label = "Javaés River", angle=80, size=6) +
      annotate("text", x = -50.3, y = -11.9, label = "Bananal\nIsland", size=8) +
      coord_equal() +
      theme_bw(base_size = 22) + xlab("") + ylab("") +
      geom_point(data=station, aes(lat, long), color="red", size=5, alpha=0.9) +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(-54,-45,1), labels=c(paste(seq(54,45,-1),"°W", sep="")))+
      scale_y_continuous(breaks=seq(-13,-5,2), labels=c(paste(seq(13,5,-2),"°S", sep="")))

grid.newpage()
v1 <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.33, y = 0.5)  #plot area for the main map
v2 <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.82, y = 0.5)  #plot area for the inset map
print(m1, vp=v1)
print(m2, vp=v2)

Here in RStudio the figure is scrambled in the "plots" section, but gets perfect when I maximize the window (i.e. click on "zoom"). By saving the figure through the zoom window I learn its "optimal" dimensions, in this case 1920x1017. However, the final dpi of the figure saved this way is low and therefore the figure is blurred (not sharp) when inserted on a Word document. Also, most journals require figures with resolution of 300ppi.

The solution for this would be increasing the resolution of the image, which is also the best for publications, but then this is when the problem really starts:

ppi <- 600
png("Tocantins_map.png", width = 1920, height = 1017, units = "px", res = ppi)
grid.newpage()
v1 <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.33, y = 0.5)  #plot area for the main map
v2 <- viewport(width = 1, height = 1, x = 0.82, y = 0.5)  #plot area for the inset map
print(m1, vp=v1)
print(m2, vp=v2)
dev.off()

The figure with a higher resolution of 600dpi is totally messed up, with weird figure placement and disproportionade text label sizes.

Is there any generic solution, or a rule of thumb, to determine the optimal figure dimensions in cases like this?

Many thanks in advance,
--
Thiago V. dos Santos
PhD student
Land and Atmospheric Science
University of Minnesota
http://www.laas.umn.edu/CurrentStudents/MeettheStudents/ThiagodosSantos/index.htm
Phone: (612) 323 9898
